Name: Severity Matrix Definition
Symptom: Need to classify incidents by impact and urgency
Root Cause: Lack of agreed severity criteria and escalation thresholds
Mitigation: Publish measurable impact and urgency criteria with escalation owners; SEV1-SEV4 is one local convention rather than a universal standard; declare early and reassess as scope changes; treat this CSV's severity labels as examples; escalate suspected security or data-loss events to the relevant response teams
Communication Template: SEV[N] - [Service]. Confirmed impact: [scope]. Unknowns: [details]. Status: Investigating. Recovery ETA: unknown unless evidence supports an estimate. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was severity based on observed impact? 2. Was escalation timely? 3. Were changes in scope recorded? 4. Were security and data risks assessed? 5. Were response targets agreed before the incident?

Name: IMOC/Incident Commander Role
Symptom: Chaotic incident response with no clear ownership
Root Cause: No designated incident commander; uncoordinated changes obscure incident state
Mitigation: Name one incident commander; delegate operations and communications as staffing allows; commander retains undelegated roles but should prioritize coordination; route system changes through the operations lead and record actions in a live incident document
Communication Template: Commander: @[name]. Operations: @[name]. Communications: @[name]. Confirmed impact: [scope or unknown]. Incident document: [link]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was command explicit? 2. Were operational changes coordinated? 3. Were roles delegated before overload? 4. Were actions and outcomes recorded? 5. Was command handoff acknowledged?

Name: Database Failover Incident
Symptom: Primary database unavailable; writes failing; replica freshness uncertain
Root Cause: Possible host or network failure; resource exhaustion; transaction recovery delays; cause depends on deployment
Mitigation: Check database events and deployment type before intervention; RDS Multi-AZ DB instance failover changes endpoint DNS and requires reconnecting clients; do not assume every replica is a failover target; use the provider runbook or fence the old primary before self-managed promotion; verify a single writer and safe transaction retries before restoring traffic
Communication Template: SEV1 - [Database] writes degraded. Failover state: [observed state]. Read availability: [verified scope or unknown]. Data-loss assessment: [unknown or evidence]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Which deployment and failover trigger applied? 2. What delayed recovery? 3. Did DNS caches and connection pools refresh? 4. Were uncertain commits reconciled? 5. What data loss was verified and when did writes recover?

Name: Kafka Consumer Lag Spike
Symptom: Consumer group falling behind; processing delay exceeding service objective
Root Cause: Possible slow processing or downstream saturation; traffic spike; skewed partitions; repeated rebalances
Mitigation: Inspect per-partition offsets and event age plus processing and rebalance metrics; for ordinary consumer groups scale only within partition parallelism and downstream capacity; tune max.poll.records and max.poll.interval.ms to measured processing time; do not blindly add partitions or reset offsets to latest; check retention headroom before claiming no loss
Communication Template: SEV2 - [Consumer group] processing delayed. Offset lag: [value]. Oldest pending event age: [measured or unknown]. Retention risk: [assessment]. Mitigation: [actual action]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was lag concentrated in hot partitions? 2. Did polling timeouts cause rebalances? 3. Was downstream capacity available? 4. Were retention and offset resets checked? 5. Were replay duplicates and ordering effects assessed?

Name: Memory Leak in Production
Symptom: Memory grows over time; OOM kills or repeated restarts reduce capacity
Root Cause: Possible retained objects or unbounded caches; rising in-flight work or native allocations can resemble a heap leak
Mitigation: Compare RSS and heap trends with traffic and release changes; reduce load and canary a compatible rollback or controlled restart while preserving serving capacity; capture diagnostics only on an instance whose loss is tolerable; Node.js heap snapshots block the main thread and can double heap use and crash the process; restrict snapshot access
Communication Template: SEV2 - [Service] memory pressure affects [verified scope]. Mitigation: [actual action]. Leak cause: [suspected or confirmed]. Recovery under observation. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was OOM confirmed? 2. Did growth persist at comparable load? 3. Were native and heap memory distinguished? 4. Did diagnostics or restarts worsen availability? 5. Was the fix verified beyond temporary restart relief?

Name: Certificate Expiration
Symptom: TLS handshakes fail for affected endpoints or clients
Root Cause: Possible expired served certificate; failed renewal; application did not reload renewed certificate
Mitigation: Inspect the certificate actually served and its hostname and chain; repair issuer or renewal failures; with cert-manager use supported renewal tooling rather than deleting the TLS Secret; verify application reload and external TLS handshakes; never bypass certificate validation; monitor renewal failures and expiry using actual certificate lifetime rather than universal day thresholds
Communication Template: SEV1 - TLS failures affect [verified endpoints or clients]. Certificate renewal state: [state]. Served certificate verification: [pending or complete]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was the expired certificate actually being served? 2. Did renewal or deployment fail? 3. Was application reload verified? 4. Did monitoring cover every TLS termination point? 5. Are renewal margins suitable for issued lifetimes?

Name: DNS Resolution Failure
Symptom: Hostname lookups fail or return inconsistent addresses; connectivity is affected
Root Cause: Possible resolver or authoritative failure; delegation or DNSSEC error; stale cached answers; network filtering
Mitigation: Compare affected resolver responses with authoritative data; distinguish NXDOMAIN and SERVFAIL from timeouts; inspect delegation and DNSSEC validation and recent changes; repair or roll back the verified fault; respect cache TTLs and private DNS boundaries; use only rehearsed fallback routing that preserves hostname and TLS validation; do not hardcode service IPs as a general fix
Communication Template: SEV1 - DNS failures affect [domains and verified client scope]. Observed response: [code or timeout]. Cause: [unknown or confirmed]. Mitigation: [actual action]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was the fault recursive or authoritative? 2. Were delegation and DNSSEC checked? 3. Did caches explain inconsistent recovery? 4. Were private zones preserved? 5. Was recovery verified from affected networks?

Name: Cascading Failure
Symptom: Failures spread across dependencies as successful throughput falls
Root Cause: Possible resource exhaustion amplified by retries; traffic redistribution; cold caches or restart loops
Mitigation: Identify the triggering change and protect remaining capacity; use tested load shedding or degraded modes and pause noncritical batch work; cap retries with jitter and deadlines; do not shift traffic to an already saturated target or restart the whole fleet; stabilize dependencies and gradually restore traffic while measuring useful throughput
Communication Template: SEV1 - [Services] degraded. Trigger: [suspected or confirmed]. Load shedding or degraded mode: [actual state]. User impact: [scope]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. What triggered and amplified the failure? 2. Were retries bounded? 3. Did failover or restarts spread overload? 4. Was recovery load ramped gradually? 5. Which overload protections need testing?

Name: Deployment Rollback
Symptom: Error rate or latency rises after a release or configuration change
Root Cause: Possible code regression; incompatible persisted data or protocol change; configuration error
Mitigation: Halt rollout and identify the change; use a tested feature disable or rollback only to a version compatible with current schema and persisted data; reverting binaries does not undo data mutations; if rollback is unsafe contain impact and prepare a reviewed forward fix or repair; verify user-facing health; test mixed-version upgrade and downgrade paths before future releases
Communication Template: SEV2 - [Service] degraded after [change]. Recovery action: [rollback or containment or forward fix]. Compatibility check: [result]. Recovery ETA: [unknown or evidence-based estimate]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Which change correlated with impact? 2. Was the rollback target data-compatible? 3. Were mixed versions tested? 4. Did canary signals reflect user impact? 5. Did any data require separate repair?

Name: Cloud Region Outage
Symptom: Regional service availability is impaired across multiple zones
Root Cause: Possible regional provider failure or workload-wide dependency failure; verify scope before declaring region loss
Mitigation: Invoke the rehearsed DR plan against agreed RPO and RTO; verify recovery-region capacity and dependencies plus data freshness; require an authorized failover decision because false automatic triggers can cause data loss; enforce the topology's write-ownership or conflict rules before routing traffic; use prepared recovery controls; fail back only after resynchronization and consistency checks
Communication Template: SEV1 - [Region] workload impaired. Provider cause: [confirmed or unknown]. Recovery destination: [region]. RPO target: [value]. Observed recovery point: [time or unknown]. Data loss: [under assessment]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was regional scope confirmed? 2. Who authorized failover? 3. Were capacity and write ownership verified? 4. What recovery time and data loss were measured versus targets? 5. Was failback or continued recovery-region operation planned?

Name: Rate Limiting Incident
Symptom: Legitimate users receive throttling or false-positive bans
Root Cause: Possible incorrect aggregation key or threshold; shared IP addresses; legitimate bursts or abusive traffic
Mitigation: Inspect matched rules and request logs; check key aggregation and trusted identity boundaries; preview scoped threshold changes where supported and retain overload protection; avoid blanket partner exemptions; return HTTP 429 where appropriate with Retry-After when known and supported; retry only safe operations within a bounded jittered retry budget
Communication Template: SEV3 - Throttling affects [verified clients or endpoints]. Adjustment: [actual scoped action]. Honor Retry-After when present; retry only operations safe to repeat. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Which rule and key caused false positives? 2. Was traffic legitimate or abusive? 3. Did changes preserve capacity? 4. Were retry behavior and ban duration checked? 5. Were temporary exceptions removed?

Name: Data Corruption
Symptom: Stored data violates application invariants or downstream results are incorrect
Root Cause: Possible faulty writer or migration; race condition; corruption propagated through replicas and derived data
Mitigation: Contain the suspected writer and affected propagation paths under incident command; preserve evidence and recovery points; determine the affected time window and records; replication is not a backup; validate a clean restore or scoped repair separately before cutover; reconcile legitimate later writes and downstream data; involve security and privacy responders when indicated
Communication Template: SEV1 - Data integrity issue affects [confirmed scope]. Containment: [verified state or pending]. Extent and recoverability: [under assessment]. Recovery point: [known or unknown]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. What evidence bounded the corruption window? 2. Was containment effective? 3. Were recovery copies free of the defect? 4. Were cross-store invariants and legitimate later writes checked? 5. Were affected users and downstream owners informed?

Name: Third-Party API Outage
Symptom: External dependency calls fail or time out; dependent features degrade
Root Cause: Possible provider failure or local DNS/TLS/authentication/network issue; excessive retries magnify impact
Mitigation: Verify local connectivity and provider status; enforce connection and request deadlines with bounded jittered retries at one layer; retry side-effecting calls only with documented idempotency and reconcile unknown outcomes; use tested circuit breaking or retry throttling; enable only approved stale-data or degraded responses; do not bypass authorization or report uncertain writes as successful
Communication Template: SEV2 - [Feature] degraded while calls to [dependency] fail. Provider cause: [confirmed or unknown]. Fallback: [verified behavior or unavailable]. Transaction outcomes: [assessment]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was the dependency actually at fault? 2. Were retries amplifying load? 3. Were uncertain side effects reconciled? 4. Were fallback freshness and permissions appropriate? 5. Was recovery gradual and verified?

Name: Blameless Postmortem Process
Root Cause: Blame discourages reporting; contributing conditions and corrective actions remain unexamined
Mitigation: Define postmortem triggers and a local review schedule; preserve the incident timeline and distinguish evidence from hypotheses; examine system conditions without assigning personal blame; review and share a sanitized report; track prioritized corrective actions with owners and due dates and verify completion; a universal 48-hour deadline is not established by the source
Communication Template: Postmortem owner: [name]. Impact and timeline: [verified summary]. Open questions: [list]. Review date: [local target]. Follow-up actions: [tracker link].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Were contributing factors evidence-backed? 2. Did the review avoid blame? 3. Were impact and response gaps captured? 4. Are actions assigned and measurable? 5. Were earlier actions completed and effective?

Name: Status Page Communication
Symptom: Customers lack reliable incident updates; support demand increases
Root Cause: No designated communications lead or prepared channels and update cadence
Mitigation: Acknowledge known impact promptly through preplanned channels; assign a communications lead and publish a next-update time even when the cause or ETA is unknown; separate confirmed facts from hypotheses; agree cadence and postmortem publication targets locally rather than universal 5-minute or 48-hour promises; coordinate sensitive disclosures with security and legal responders; verify recovery before declaring resolution
Communication Template: Status: [Investigating|Identified|Monitoring|Resolved]. Confirmed impact: [scope]. Mitigation: [actual action]. Unknowns: [details]. Recovery ETA: [unknown or supported estimate]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Did updates meet agreed targets? 2. Did they state known impact and uncertainty? 3. Were promised updates sent even without progress? 4. Was recovery verified before resolution? 5. Were affected customers and support teams informed?

Name: Split-Brain Containment and Writer Fencing
Symptom: Multiple nodes appear writable after a network partition or failover
Root Cause: Old primary was not fenced; reachability was mistaken for proof of failure; promotion authority was ambiguous
Mitigation: For a single-writer topology stop unsafe writes and establish authoritative ownership using the tested HA runbook; verify the old primary cannot accept writes before promoting another node; DNS changes alone do not fence a writer; do not promote when fencing cannot be confirmed; preserve divergent data for reconciliation and rebuild or resynchronize the former primary before rejoining
Communication Template: SEV1 - Conflicting writer state suspected in [cluster]. Write containment: [verified or pending]. Authoritative writer: [confirmed identity or unknown]. Divergence: [under assessment]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was fencing verified independently of DNS? 2. Who authorized promotion? 3. Were writes accepted on both sides? 4. Was divergent history preserved and reconciled? 5. Was the former primary safely rejoined as a standby?

Name: Point-in-Time Recovery Verification
Symptom: Restore completes but data correctness or application recovery remains uncertain
Root Cause: Backup success was mistaken for recoverability; selected recovery point or restored configuration is unsuitable
Mitigation: Choose a verified clean point within the available recovery window; restore to an isolated target and retain the source; RDS DB instance PITR creates a new instance rather than rewinding the source; verify security and parameter groups plus application invariants and dependencies; reconcile later valid writes and external side effects before approved cutover; measure recovery time and gradually admit traffic
Communication Template: SEV1 - [Service] recovery in progress. Selected recovery point: [time UTC]. Data validation: [state]. Configuration validation: [state]. Data-loss window: [assessed or unknown]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was the selected point before corruption? 2. Was the available restore window verified? 3. Were restored configuration and cross-store consistency checked? 4. Were later writes and side effects reconciled? 5. Did end-to-end recovery meet objectives?

Name: Incident Shift Handoff
Symptom: Long-running response loses ownership or repeats failed mitigations during shift changes
Root Cause: Fatigue or implicit handoff; stale incident document; pending work lacks owners
Mitigation: Arrange relief before responders are overloaded; brief the incoming commander live on impact and hypotheses plus changes and pending actions; obtain explicit acceptance before outgoing command leaves; announce the new owner to responders and update the incident document and next communication deadline
Communication Template: Handoff at [time UTC]. Incoming commander: [name]. Acceptance: [confirmed]. Active risks: [summary]. Pending actions and owners: [link]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Was handoff explicitly acknowledged? 2. Were unsuccessful actions and current risks transferred? 3. Did each pending task retain an owner? 4. Were all responders told who was in command? 5. Was relief arranged in time?

Name: Incident Communications Dependency Failure
Symptom: Responders cannot reach the usual chat or incident document; status updates stall
Root Cause: Coordination tools or their access dependencies share the incident failure domain
Mitigation: Prearrange and exercise an approved fallback command channel and incident log outside the affected service; keep contact and escalation details accessible during outages; announce the active command location and communications owner; maintain timestamped decisions and updates; reconcile fallback records afterward without exposing credentials or customer data
Communication Template: Primary coordination channel unavailable. Approved fallback: [channel]. Commander: [name]. Communications owner: [name]. Public impact update: [safe link or message]. Next update: [time UTC].
Postmortem Checklist: 1. Which shared dependency blocked coordination? 2. Could responders access fallback contacts? 3. Was one active command location clear? 4. Were decisions and customer updates preserved? 5. Were fallback records reconciled securely?
